title: Review of the Effects of Rare Earth Element Additions to Magnesium Alloys on Biocompatibility: An Evaluation from Mechanical, Corrosion, and Biological Perspectives
abstract: Abstract Rare earth elements (REE), the subject of this study, have become a growing focus of interest in biomaterials research in recent years, particularly in magnesium (Mg) and high-entropy alloys (HEA). These studies demonstrate that the addition of REE’s can significantly improve the microstructure of Mg alloys and, consequently, their mechanical properties, corrosion resistance and biocompatibility. For this reason, a large number of studies conducted in recent years have sought to understand the effects of REE additions on the mechanical properties, corrosion behaviour and biological responses of magnesium alloys. In this review, the effects of rare-earth element additions on the biocompatibility of magnesium alloys have been comprehensively examined in light of recent studies, and current developments and future research directions have been discussed using the review method. This comprehensive review systematically evaluates the effects of REE additions on the microstructural evolution, corrosion behaviour, mechanical performance and biocompatibility of magnesium alloys. An analysis of the latest studies indicates that Mg -REE alloying leads to significant grain refinement, the formation of stable intermetallic phases and an increase in corrosion resistance through the development of more protective surface films; these changes result in increased mechanical strength and more favourable biological responses, including improved cell viability and reduced cytotoxicity. Furthermore, this review highlights that Mg–REE alloys are promising candidates for biodegradable implant applications. Overall, Mg–REE alloys are promising candidates for biodegradable implant applications, as they combine enhanced mechanical integrity, controlled degradation and improved biocompatibility. However, despite these advantages, it has been concluded that further research is required to determine the long-term biological interactions and optimised alloy compositions; future research should therefore focus on in vivo performance and the development of alloy systems optimised for clinical use.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The desire to lead a long and healthy life, one of humanity’s age-old goals, has seen significant progress in recent years thanks to advancements in modern medicine and materials science. Since ancient times, people have sought to restore the functionality of body parts affected by trauma or disease. However, these advancements have also brought new challenges in the fields of medicine and materials science. An increasingly ageing population is leading to a rise in the incidence of age-related diseases. Furthermore, changes in modern dietary habits compared to previous generations are contributing to the spread of obesity and various metabolic disorders. Furthermore, the growing interest in high-risk recreational sports—which carry risks ranging from fractures to serious internal injuries-is giving rise to different health issues. In this context, the medicine and materials science of today and the future must adapt to the changing dynamics of modern society.

The human body and its associated biological systems are extremely complex and unique, comprising a system that is even more intricate than the most advanced machines. The human body contains 206 bones and over 300 joints; 1  throughout history, people have sought to develop solutions to restore the functionality of body parts damaged by trauma or disease. The first attempt at orthopaedic treatment of a bone fracture was made in the sixteenth century. 2 , 3  In developed countries, the ageing population has shown a marked and accelerating increase, particularly in recent years. This demographic shift has led to a significant increase in the use of implants, driven by the need to maintain the quality of life and enable individuals in the older age group to continue their daily activities. Furthermore, urgent needs have arisen to address clinical challenges encountered in fields such as vascular treatments, trauma management, cardiology, dentistry, orthopaedics and wound care. To meet these requirements, one of the medical community’s primary focuses has been the development of high-performance implantable biomaterials. Indeed, the biomaterials market has grown from US$95 billion in 2011 to US$135 billion in 2017. 4  The global biomaterials market is projected to reach US$236.99 billion by 2025 and US$836.54 billion by 2033, expanding at a compound annual growth rate of 17.25% between 2026 and 2033. 5  In particular, the rise in the prevalence of musculoskeletal conditions and chronic skeletal diseases is expected to drive market growth by increasing demand for biomaterial-based implants. 6

Humans have been using metallic implants since ancient times to live longer, healthier lives. However, with advancing technology, and particularly over the last twenty years, there has been a growing interest in the application of biofunctional design principles compared to more traditional bio-inert implants. 7  In this context, one of the most intriguing areas has been the development of biodegradable magnesium (Mg) alloy implants for orthopaedic and cardiovascular repair. 8  Biomedical materials are biomaterials that are produced or processed to be suitable for use as medical devices or their components, and are generally intended to be in prolonged contact with biological materials. 9  In recent years, there has been a strong research focus on the development and selection of multifunctional biomaterials. In this context, temporary scaffold materials used in tissue engineering not only provide structural support, but also enable the transport and release of critical biological components such as fibroblasts, morphogenetic protein-2 and endothelial growth factors. Examples of such multifunctional biomaterials include magnesium-based implants, which exhibit mechanical properties such as sufficient tensile strength and fracture resistance. 10 , 11

Apart from medicines, a biomaterial is defined as any substance or combination of substances, whether synthetic or of natural origin, which can be used for any duration to partially or completely support or alter any tissue, organ or function of the body, with the aim of maintaining or improving an individual’s quality of life. 12  Biocompatibility is the ability of a material to remain biologically harmless when applied to a living organism. 13  Magnesium is an element that is well tolerated by the body, possessing extremely low toxicity and rapid excretion. 14  Mg exhibits numerous bioactive effects in the body, including improving bone formation and protecting against oxidative stress, 15 , 16  and Mg alloys can degrade in vivo in such a way as to allow the implant to be completely removed without surgical intervention. This prevents the need for revision surgery and eliminates concerns regarding thrombosis associated with permanent implants. 17  Optimizing the alloy composition is a widely accepted approach for improving and controlling the corrosion behaviour of biodegradable orthopaedic implants. This is of particular critical importance for Mg-based biomaterials, which exhibit high degradation rates in vivo and result in the release of hydrogen gas; as these two effects can lead to a reduction in the implant’s mechanical integrity before the healing process of the fractured tissue is complete. 18

Magnesium-based alloys are of particular interest due to their low density and elastic modulus similar to that of bone, which enables them to exhibit mechanical behaviour similar to natural bone tissue; consequently, they have gained exceptional importance in recent years as potential candidates for biodegradable implants. 19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 – 23  Mg has high biocompatibility, 24 , 25  is easily resorbable and is completely degraded in vivo. Its metabolic products are magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, which can be excreted via the metabolic pathway. 19 , 26 , 27  Furthermore, Mg is an essential trace element for the human body, acting as a key cofactor in many enzymatic reactions and playing a vital role in energy metabolism. 28  At the same time, Mg closely resembles the biomechanical properties of human bone, making it an ideal bone repair material, 29  and is also associated with bone health. 30 , 31  The fact that they can degrade within the body without the need for a second surgical intervention following implantation makes Mg alloys attractive candidates for biodegradable implants. However, as Mg and its alloys are not inherently bioactive, their interaction with bone tissue remains limited. Consequently, surface modification and structural design approaches emerge as key strategies for controlling degradation rates and improving the bone–implant interface. In particular, Mg alloys with porous structures offer superior potential in biomedical applications as scaffold materials that support bone growth, cell migration and the reduction of the stress shield effect. 19 , 32  Particularly due to their high specific strength, elastic moduli similar to those of bone tissue, and their ability to degrade within the body, interest in the use of Mg alloys as biodegradable materials in bone implants is growing day by day. 33 ,  34 ,  35 ,  36 ,  37 – 38  Alongside advancing technologies, the growing demand for biodegradable materials has further accelerated research in this field within orthopaedic and cardiovascular applications. 39  However, magnesium alloys are susceptible to various degradation mechanisms, including galvanic corrosion, localized corrosion, friction corrosion, stress corrosion cracking and corrosion fatigue. 40

As mentioned above, researchers today have focussed on the development of various biomedical Mg alloys and are conducting extensive studies on the microstructure and properties of these alloys. 41 , 42  Among these alloys, Mg alloys containing Rare Earth Elements (REE) are attracting significant interest due to their superior performance. In particular, the addition of REE elements to Mg as alloying elements significantly enhances the mechanical properties of Mg alloys through mechanisms such as fine-grain strengthening, precipitation strengthening, solid-solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening. 43 , 44  REE makes a major contribution to both the mechanical and corrosion and biological properties of Mg alloys and is therefore widely used in alloys for a wide variety of applications. 45  Magnesium is one of the most abundant elements in the human body, with almost half of it found in bone tissue. 46  Due to its active role in bone metabolism and osteogenic processes, magnesium alloys are considered highly desirable materials for biodegradable implants. 47 ,  48 ,  49 ,  50 ,  51 – 52  However, magnesium’s susceptibility to rapid corrosion in physiological environments due to high chloride ion concentrations can lead to premature loss of mechanical strength and implant failure. 53 ,  54 – 55  This rapid degradation behaviour observed in Mg alloys results in an early decline in mechanical properties, hydrogen gas release and rapid mass loss. 56 ,  57 ,  58 ,  59 ,  60 – 61  Although it has been reported that Mg and its alloys promote bone formation, 62 ,  63 ,  64 – 65  most existing alloys exhibit a significant loss of strength in the early stages of degradation, and this poses a significant limitation for orthopaedic applications where the healing process can take months. 55 , 66  Mg’s low intrinsic potential tends to lead to the formation of intermetallic phases with higher galvanic potentials, which in turn results in accelerated cathodic kinetics. Most alloying elements impair the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys. 67 , 68  As many Mg alloys corrode very rapidly, this leads to the early loss of the alloy’s mechanical integrity, rendering them unsuitable for clinical orthopaedic applications. 69 , 70  Therefore, improving the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys is of great importance for clinical applications. However, efforts are being made to overcome these issues through advancements in production technology, alloying with different elements, and surface treatments. 71

Mg is an essential nutrient for maintaining human health; it promotes bone growth, enhances cell adhesion to biomaterials, and aids in the differentiation of osteoblasts and biomineralization. 72  Furthermore, due to their active chemical behaviour, Mg alloys corrode readily in a physiological environment and can therefore degrade to produce magnesium hydroxide [Mg(OH) 2 ] and hydrogen (H 2 ). 73 , 74  Compared to other metal implants, it has been demonstrated that the corrosion products of Mg alloys are non-toxic and can be excreted from the body via human metabolism. 75

Magnesium (Mg) is one of the best-studied biodegradable metals, widely used in cardiovascular and orthopaedic applications. 76  This biodegradable metal offers excellent in vivo biocompatibility, possesses the mechanical strength required to provide support to bone undergoing the regeneration process, and exhibits a controlled degradation profile. It has been found that the mechanical behaviour of biodegradable metals is far superior to that of biodegradable polymers. 77  Among other candidate biodegradable materials, magnesium possesses high specific strength, as well as a relatively lower density and elastic modulus. 78  The elastic modulus of Mg is approximately 41 GPa, and its density is 1.75 g/cm 3 . These properties are very close to those of bone, thereby helping to minimize the risk associated with stress shielding. 79

The sole purpose of biodegradable materials is to provide short-term support for the healing process of damaged or injured tissue prior to their degradation. For this concept to be effective, the materials must possess mechanical properties suitable for their intended applications and sufficient corrosion resistance to ensure gradual degradation. As next-generation biomaterials, these materials must also possess satisfactory properties in terms of both bioactivity and biocompatibility within the human body. 22  When magnesium is alloyed with elements such as REE, which are used as strengthening elements, it gains high strength and improved mechanical, metallurgical and tribological properties thanks to grain refinement and the strong solid-solution strengthening mechanisms of the alloying elements. This contributes to the development of Mg-REE alloys, which, due to their biodegradability in a physiological environment-that is, within the human body-represent a promising alternative for permanent bone implants. 80

Nowadays, permanent metal implants made from stainless steel, cobalt-chromium, and titanium alloys are widely used in the treatment of bone fractures. 81 , 82  Although these implants offer sufficient mechanical strength and corrosion resistance, they generally need to be removed from the body via a second surgical procedure within 1–2 years after bone healing is complete. 83 ,  84 – 85  This situation entails both additional costs and the risk of a new surgical procedure for patients. Various interactions and reactions between implants and the human body can lead to metallic implants releasing ions that may interfere with the physiological movement of ions in nerve cells; furthermore, the accumulation of metallic ions in the human body can cause local adverse tissue reactions and allergic reactions. This, in turn, can lead to injuries and surgical failures. 86  Over the years, numerous studies have been conducted to develop implants from various Mg alloys with biodegradable properties, with the aim of overcoming the problems caused by permanent metal implants. 87 , 88  In particular, in recent years, biomedical Mg alloy implants have been widely used in clinical settings to repair bone tissue defects. In particular, biodegradable and bioabsorbable metals such as magnesium, iron (Fe) and zinc (Zn) dissolve in a controlled manner in the physiological environment and are either absorbed by the organism or eliminated naturally, in parallel with the healing process of the surrounding tissue. Thanks to these properties, these materials eliminate the need for a secondary surgical removal. 89 , 90  The fact that these types of implants degrade naturally within the body eliminates the need for a second surgical procedure to remove the implant, thereby reducing both treatment costs and the risk of post-operative complications, as well as the physical and psychological burden on patients. 91 , 92  Within this group of materials, magnesium alloys-which are predominantly alloyed with REE elements-are among the leading candidates for orthopaedic implant applications due to their superior biocompatibility, osteopromotive effects  93 , 94  and mechanical properties similar to those of human bone. 95 , 96  Furthermore, these alloys enhance biomechanical compatibility by minimizing the stress shielding effect that arises during load transfer at the bone-implant interface. 77  In terms of degradation behaviour, alloying with REE elements effectively increases the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys. 97 , 98  However, the adhesion of bacteria to the implant surface and the resulting infection and inflammation pose a significant challenge. In contrast, REE elements offer an extremely efficient, long-lasting and cost-effective solution for antibacterial materials. They exhibit exceptional broad-spectrum bactericidal capabilities. 40

The field of biomaterials is becoming increasingly important with each passing day due to the high demands of an ageing population and the rise in average body weight. 99  However, biomaterials used in medical applications must possess a number of critical properties simultaneously in order to function safely within the human body. Firstly, it is of great importance that these materials are biocompatible, meaning they do not cause any harmful effects when interacting with living tissues; this includes potential effects on cellular structures, bone tissue and the chemical balance of bodily fluids. Furthermore, biomaterials must be non-toxic; genotoxic or cytotoxic effects can lead to implant rejection and serious health issues. From a mechanical perspective, the combination of a low elastic modulus with high strength contributes to the implant’s longevity and helps prevent the formation of a stress shield in the bone. Furthermore, high wear resistance and a low coefficient of friction prevent the implant from loosening and the formation of wear particles that could cause inflammation in surrounding tissues. Given the human body’s saline and oxygen-rich environment, it is essential that biomaterials possess high corrosion resistance; otherwise, the release of metal ions could cause toxic effects. In addition, due to the repetitive movements of the joints, the material must have a long fatigue life; otherwise, implant fractures may occur. Finally, osseointegration—the formation of a direct and strong bond between the implant and living bone-is a critical factor for the stability and success of the implant, particularly in bone implants. Numerous parameters, such as material type, alloy composition and manufacturing method, directly influence this process. 9 , 22 , 100 ,  101 – 102

The mechanical performance, degradation behaviour and microstructure of magnesium-based alloys can be significantly modified by the addition of various non-toxic elements such as aluminium (Al), silicon (Si), bismuth (Bi), silver (Ag), zirconium (Zr), lithium (Li) and tin (Sn), as well as strontium (Sr), Calcium (Ca), Zinc (Zn), Manganese (Mn) and Rare Earth (RE) elements, can be significantly altered. 103 ,  104 ,  105 ,  106 – 107  The fundamental requirements for materials to be used in biomedical applications are sufficient mechanical strength, controlled degradation behaviour and high biocompatibility; the most important of these relates to the use of alloys formed by Mg and REE in biomaterials. 108 ,  109 ,  110 ,  111 ,  112 ,  113 ,  114 ,  115 ,  116 ,  117 – 118  It has been demonstrated that Mg–REE alloys have a positive effect on angiogenesis when used as implants. For example, Zhou et al. 119  reported that Mg–Li–Al–REE alloys increased the viability of human umbilical cord vein endothelial cells. Similarly, Tang et al. 120  demonstrated that Mg–Sr–REE alloys promote the proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells. The solid solubility of the element Neodymium (Nd) in Mg alloys is only 3.6%, and the precipitation of a second phase in Mg alloys is easy, which can increase alloy strength via precipitation hardening. At the same time, Nd dissolved in the Mg matrix can increase the corrosion potential of the matrix, reduce the potential difference with the second phase, and prevent galvanic corrosion. 121 , 122  The addition of small amounts of the elements cerium (Ce), praseodymium (Pr), erbium (Er) and yttrium (Y) (mass fraction 1%) can effectively increase the strength of Mg-REE alloys, but when the content of alloying elements reaches 3%, the ultimate tensile strength decreases. For Mg-Er alloys, however, the ultimate tensile strength decreases when the Er content reaches 10%. The addition of Y elements can significantly increase the plastic deformation capacity of magnesium alloys. 123  Strontium (Sr) is an alkaline earth metal that plays a vital role in the human body by promoting the growth of osteoblasts and preventing bone resorption. Traces of strontium are found in the bones and teeth of the human body, where it accumulates to enhance bone growth. Recent research has demonstrated that strontium aids in bone remodelling by stimulating osteoclasts. Furthermore, researchers have reported that adding Sr to form an alloy with Mg enhances the mechanical, tribological and corrosion properties of the Mg alloy. Furthermore, alloying Sr with Mg can improve grain structure and reduce shrinkage, increase porosity, and lead to improved tribological, corrosion and mechanical properties by increasing the relative density of Mg-Sr alloy castings. 124

Alloying elements added to Mg have varying effects on corrosion. Nd increases the corrosion rate at low concentrations but reduces it at high concentrations. Ce reduces the corrosion rate by refining the eutectic structure and forming a protective oxide film. Lanthanum (La) increases corrosion resistance by forming an amorphous phase with superior corrosion resistance. Gadolinium (Gd) accelerates anodic reactions and increases the corrosion rate. Y increases corrosion resistance by refining the grains and reducing impurities in the Mg melt. Dysprosium (Dy) exhibits filiform corrosion at low concentrations and pitting corrosion at higher concentrations. 40  The addition of REE elements to Mg consistently increases strength, ductility and mechanical stability, largely due to the microstructural refinement and stabilization imparted by these elements. In terms of biological properties, Mg-REE alloys demonstrate commendable biocompatibility, which is essential for any biomaterial designed for medical use. In this context, REE elements such as Ce, La, Nd, Y, thorium (Th), Gd and scandium (Sc) are widely used to improve the mechanical, corrosion and biological properties of Mg alloys. 125  However, some REE’s present a complex picture. Whilst Y exhibits good biocompatibility, La and Gd may be cytotoxic at higher concentrations. 126  Therefore, optimizing the concentration of these REE’s is crucial in order to balance their beneficial effects on bone growth against potential cytotoxicity.

REE’s have high solid-state solubility in Mg and offer a significant advantage in improving the performance of Mg alloys. 127  Lighter REE elements such as La, Ce, praseodymium (Pr), Nd and europium (Eu) have lower solid-state solubility in Mg, and the intermetallic compounds they form are primarily distributed at grain boundaries, thereby providing second-phase precipitation strengthening. Heavier REE elements such as Gd, Dy and Y primarily strengthen Mg alloys via solid solution. Studies have found that, in addition to traditional strengthening effects, REE’s can effectively refine the grain structure; REE’s can also improve the oxide film structure on the surface of Mg alloys, thereby increasing film density and thus enhancing corrosion resistance. 128  Relevant studies have confirmed that rare earth elements such as La, Ce, Y, Nd, Gd and erbium (Er) can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the alloy matrix by increasing the density of hydroxides or oxides following the degradation of the Mg alloy. 129  The role of REE elements in altering the biological degradation mechanism of magnesium alloys is crucial for their successful application in biomedical implants. REE elements such as Ce, La, Nd and Y significantly influence the degradation pathways of magnesium alloys by forming protective oxide layers, improving microstructure and reducing hydrogen gas formation. Ce forms a stable cerium oxide layer that acts as a physical barrier and reduces corrosion rates. Lanthanum promotes a more homogeneous phase distribution, leading to a less porous and more stable oxide layer. Nd stabilizes the oxide layer and mitigates hydrogen embrittlement by reducing hydrogen formation. It regulates grain size, improves mechanical properties and enhances corrosion resistance. 40  The literature indicates that REE elements enhance the strength and creep resistance of Mg alloys through grain refinement, solid solution and precipitation hardening mechanisms; they also improve corrosion resistance in corrosive environments by forming a passive film. 130 , 131  In particular, when REE is added to magnesium alloys as a primary alloying element, the alloy’s strength and creep resistance are significantly improved, which has encouraged the development of the Mg-REE alloy series. Consequently, the high-performance cast magnesium alloys developed today are primarily Mg-REE alloys. 132 ,  133 – 134

It is also essential that the implant material is mechanically strong enough to withstand various biomechanical stresses—such as yield strength, Young’s modulus, tensile strength and compressive strength—which are of critical importance for load-bearing applications. Furthermore, the ideal implant material should be lightweight, wear-resistant and suitable for bone integration. The increasing use of orthopaedic devices, such as joint prostheses and internal fixators, is contributing to an increase in life expectancy. Research into biomaterials is crucial for enhancing implant performance, improving function, delivering bioactive compounds and achieving tissue regeneration goals. Biodegradable materials are attracting interest due to their mechanical properties similar to cortical bone, high biodegradability, and compatibility with diagnostic imaging for healing assessments. In this specific context, magnesium-based alloys are attracting significant interest due to their numerous desirable properties when compared to other materials. 135  These properties of Mg-REE alloys make REE-alloyed Mg alloys a promising option for biomedical applications. In this context, the grain refinement, precipitation hardening, stable phase formation and micro control, it is believed that the disadvantages of Mg alloys-such as mechanical weakness, rapid corrosion, low yield strength, limited ductility, and high-temperature instability-which currently limit their use in critical environments, 136 , 137  can be overcome. 112 ,  113 ,  114 ,  115 ,  116 ,  117 – 118 , 125 , 130 ,  131 ,  132 ,  133 ,  134 ,  135 ,  136 ,  137 – 138  However, the mechanism of action underlying the antitumour effects of REE elements has not yet been fully elucidated. Furthermore, the majority of existing studies have examined the effects of REE elements on tumour cells through in vitro experiments, whilst the number of in vivo studies is quite limited. 139

In recent years, the new Mg-REE series of alloys has been the subject of significant research. 132  There are numerous studies in the literature demonstrating the relationship between Mg-REE and biomaterials. These studies not only contribute to the literature but also fill a significant gap in the field. However, the absence of a study that evaluates the results of research on the biocompatibility of REE-containing Mg alloys and presents them in a comprehensive manner has necessitated the writing of a review article on the biocompatibility of Mg-REE alloys. In line with the objective of our study, a comprehensive literature review was conducted, using the keywords “magnesium alloys”, “rare earth elements” and “biocompatibility” as the basis. The relevant terms were searched together using the AND operator, with the aim of identifying studies directly focussed on the subject. The search was conducted on the Web of Science (all databases), Scopus, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar and Academia.edu platforms to access a broad data pool encompassing interdisciplinary studies, and a large number of studies were identified. In recent years, it has become clear that biodegradable materials have emerged as a significant area of research amongst the materials used in biomedical applications. Increasing performance requirements in materials science and engineering, rapidly advancing technologies and expanding fields of application necessitate the development of new alloy systems with superior properties that go beyond those of traditional materials. Recent bibliometric analyses reveal that research into biomaterials has experienced significant growth. Over 100,000 publications have been indexed in major scientific databases, highlighting the growing global interest in and importance of this field. In this context, biodegradable metallic materials are of particular interest for orthopaedic and cardiovascular implant applications. 140  Magnesium alloys based on Rare Earth Elements (Mg-REE) are on the cusp of revolutionizing future biomaterials, embodying the synergy of strength, biocompatibility and innovation required to redefine medical implant technology. 40

In the light of research in this field, this review study provides a comprehensive overview of the literature by identifying the benefits and limitations of REE additions to the performance of magnesium-based biomaterials.

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: REE is a group of raw materials considered indispensable for high-tech industries, comprising the lanthanides-the elements numbered 57–71 on the periodic table Lanthanum (La), Cerium (Ce), Praseodymium (Pr), Neodymium (Nd), Promethium (Pm), Samarium (Sm), Europium (Eu), Gadolinium (Gd), Terbium (Tb), Dysprosium (Dy), Holmium (Ho), Erbium (Er), Thulium (Tm), Ytterbium (Yb) and Lutetium (Lu)], and includes the elements scandium (Sc, atomic number 21) and yttrium (Y, atomic number 39), which have similar chemical properties and are typically found alongside them in nature. 141  Rising demand and limited supply have placed REE at the centre of global competition, whilst the environmental and technical challenges of extraction and processing further enhance the value of these elements. The stages of REE, from raw ore to the final product, are shown in Figure  1 , whilst Figure  2  provides images of some REE elements. Figure 1 The stages of REE from raw ore to final product. 141 Figure 2 Some rare earth elements. 141 , 142

One of the key factors determining the suitability of magnesium alloys for biomedical applications is the material’s mechanical strength and ductility. The addition of REE to Mg alloys enhances their mechanical strength by altering their microstructure. In particular, alloys containing Nd, Y and Gd elements yield more stable and fine-grained structures. 143  Additives such as Nd, Gd and Y can significantly increase both yield and tensile strength. For example, the Mg-10Gd-5Y-0.4Zr alloy has achieved a yield strength of 289 MPa. 112  In particular, the elements Y, Gd, Nd and Ce limit dislocation movement within the Mg crystal structure, leading to increases in both hardness and tensile strength. Furthermore, the precipitation hardening mechanism is activated by REE additions; fine and homogeneously distributed precipitates inhibit dislocation movement, thereby enhancing strength. The most pronounced effect of REE elements in Mg alloys arises through microstructural improvement. These elements promote the formation of second phases in the Mg matrix, leading to grain refinement; consequently, the material’s yield strength increases in accordance with the Hall–Petch relationship. 144  In their comprehensive experimental studies, Fanjin and colleagues reported that alloying elements and heat treatment play a significant role in the precipitation behaviour of Mg-REE alloys. 145  Feng and colleagues also reported in their various experimental studies that Gd/Nd additions increase tensile strength. 146  The addition of La, on the other hand, has improved strength and elongation in the AZ91 alloy. 147  These improvements occur through mechanisms such as solid solution hardening, precipitation hardening, grain refinement and texture modification. Gadolinium, a member of the REE group, has a solubility of 23.49% by weight in Mg at the eutectic temperature and exhibits a strong solid solution hardening effect. 148 , 149  Stanford et al. reported that the addition of up to 1% Gd in Mg-Gd alloys weakens the recrystallization structure, whilst at higher concentrations the structure remains largely unchanged. The same study reported that strength increased up to a 1% Gd addition, that matrix hardening occurred due to the restriction of dislocation motion, and that this mechanism did not adversely affect ductility. 150  Similarly, strength values also increased up to a 1% Gd addition by weight and remained unchanged with further additions. In a study, Stanford and Barnett reported that dissolved Gd locks the dislocation motion in the alloy following recrystallization annealing and causes matrix hardening; they concluded that such a mechanism does not affect the ductility of Mg-Gd alloys. The same authors, in the same study, stated that the addition of Gd to Mg weakens the texture and increases elongation in the extrusion direction by forming REE texture components. 151  It was also noted that the Mg-1.55Gd alloy exhibited higher ductility when extruded at 450 °C compared to 510 °C, the reason being the suppression of REE texture component formation at high extrusion temperatures. It has also been reported that tensile elongations for Mg-1%Gd increased from 4.8 to 30% following annealing between 350 and 450 °C. 152  Furthermore, gadolinium enhances hardness and tensile strength in Mg-Gd alloys by creating a grain-refining effect. 153

It has been reported that neodymium (Nd) improves high-temperature resistance and strength in Mg-Nd-Zn-Zr alloys. 154  Nd, which is part of the REE group, is the element with the highest solid solubility in Mg and the lowest eutectic temperature of 552 °C; it has been reported that the addition of Nd to Mg contributes significantly to age hardening. 155  The microstructure of Mg-Nd alloys consists of dendritic Mg and segregated Mg 12 Nd eutectic. Strength improves with increasing Nd content. This is attributed to solid solution hardening and precipitation hardening. 156

The addition of holmium (Ho) to Mg improves the microstructure in Mg-Zr-Sr-Ho alloys, thereby enhancing mechanical properties. 157  The combined use of erbium (Er) and Gd in the AM50 alloy results in increased strength and ductility. 158  Cerium (Ce), on the other hand, has a solubility in Mg that is almost negligible at room temperature and acts as an eutectic-forming element. Research and studies have shown that the use of Ce as an alloying element in Mg not only affects dispersion hardening but also contributes to intergranular eutectic hardening. 159  It has been reported that the addition of 0.2% Ce by weight to Mg increases the tensile elongation of Mg from 9.1 to 31%. 160  In this study, the increase in ductility occurred in conjunction with an increase in the 0.2% yield strength; this increase in ductility was accompanied by a slight increase in tensile strength, along with a reduction in grain size due to the addition of Ce. 161  It has been reported that the addition of 0.5% Ce by weight to Mg results in increased strength, along with greater surface oxidation and a decrease in ductility during extrusion. There is also a study indicating that a significant increase in ductility, from 2.7 to 11.9%, was observed in the Mg-1%Ce alloy following annealing at 350 °C. 152  It has been reported that when Ce is added to Mg as an alloying element, Mg 12 Ce intermetallic is formed, and regarding the decrease in ductility accompanying the increase in strength, the effect of the increase in the volume fraction of the intermetallic has a greater influence than the morphology of the intermetallic. 152 , 155  It has also been reported that REE elements increase ductility by hindering dislocation movement. 162  REE elements ensure the preservation of mechanical properties by enhancing the stability of precipitates at high temperatures. 163 , 164

Whilst Nd exhibits a moderate solid solubility of approximately 3.5% in a Mg matrix at 545 °C, Gd’s solubility in Mg is highly temperature-dependent, reaching as high as 23.49% at 548 °C. Similarly, Mg–Y alloys exhibit a relatively high solid solubility limit of approximately 13.9% at around 574 °C. In contrast, the solubility of Ce in Mg is more limited, reaching approximately 0.8% at the eutectic temperature of 595 °C. 145  Rogal and colleagues investigated the ageing effect on grain size in the Thixo-Cast EZ33 alloy containing 1.2% Ce and 0.9% Nd, and reported that the grain size of the Thixo-Cast EZ33 alloy increased by 92 µm with ageing. 165

These studies demonstrate that microstructural mechanisms such as grain refinement, phase stabilization and texture control operate in concert in Mg alloys with REE additions, thereby exhibiting multifaceted effects that balance mechanical strength and ductility. The different solubility behaviours of REE’s facilitate the formation of fine, homogeneously distributed precipitates during heat treatment in Mg-REE alloys, contributing to the emergence of characteristic ageing hardening responses.

In conclusion, REE elements improve formability and ductility in Mg alloys whilst also enhancing strength through solid solution hardening and eutectic phases. 144 , 155  The addition of REE elements has also yielded significant results in terms of improving the deformability of Mg. 166

sections.heading: Corrosion Behaviour
paragraphs: Although magnesium (Mg) and Mg-based alloys offer attractive properties as biodegradable materials, one of their most significant limitations is their high corrosion rate. In the aqueous environment of the human body, Mg alloys dissolve rapidly as a result of electrochemical reactions and lose their mechanical integrity due to uncontrolled hydrogen gas release. The addition of REE to Mg alloys enhances corrosion resistance, providing significant advantages in biomedical applications, and reduces the corrosion rate by altering the distribution and chemical composition of secondary phases. 167  Mg-Nd alloys are considered a promising alternative to traditional WE43 alloys for absorbable stent applications due to their low yield strength, low elongation ratio and limited corrosion degradation. 169  Furthermore, the high solubility of the Nd element and its ability to enhance ageing improve strength and corrosion performance through the formation of hard secondary phases such as Mg 3 Nd. 168 , 169

REE’s have a significant effect on the high-temperature resistance and creep resistance of alloys; by improving the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys, 170  they significantly enhance magnesium’s resistance to corrosion. 171  For engineering applications, REE’s are typically added as a mischmetal comprising various compositions rich in Ce, La and Nd; however, the composition of this mischmetal may vary depending on the source. 172  The addition of low levels of La, Nd and Ce to Mg alloys reduces the corrosion rate and extends the corrosion life. 23  Furthermore, it has been observed that the addition of Ce and Nd significantly influences the corrosive wear behaviour in Mg alloys, whilst localized corrosion becomes more controlled. 109

Similarly, CeO 2  nanoparticles reduce the corrosion rate by slowing down the pH increase rate in the Mg-Zn matrix. 173  However, the optimum concentration is of critical importance; for example, whilst a 10% Gd addition to Mg increases corrosion resistance, the formation of the Mg 5 Gd phase at the 15% level leads to an increase in the corrosion rate. 153

Ce improves the creep behaviour of magnesium alloys by increasing their corrosion resistance, plastic deformation capacity and strain hardening rate, whilst reducing their yield strength. 174 ,  175 – 176  In a study, Ce was observed to be concentrated at grain boundaries rather than within the grains in the alloy. This is attributed to Ce being a surface-active element within magnesium and having a positive absorption effect. The concentration of Ce at grain boundaries reduces surface energy and nucleation energy, thereby increasing the nucleation rate. 176  It has been reported that the addition of zinc (Zn) or strontium (Sr) to a Mg-3Ce-1.2Mn-1Zn alloy containing cerium has no positive or negative effect on the morphology of the Mg 12 Ce phase or its distribution within the alloy; however, it has been reported that alloys containing Zr and Sr exhibit a higher proportion of residual Mg 12 Ce phase in their structure, and that the stability of this phase positively influences creep behaviour. 177  Furthermore, there is evidence that Y and Gd additions enhance corrosion resistance by stabilizing the formation of the passive film. 178

The contribution of REE’s to corrosion resistance is also referred to as the ‘scavenger effect’. This effect is explained by the fact that harmful impurity elements, such as iron, within the alloy form compounds with alkaline earth metals, rendering them harmless and thereby reducing cathodic activity. 179  Furthermore, REE’s support corrosion control by forming thin, protective oxide layers on the surface. Consequently, the amount and distribution of REE additions are key determinants of corrosion performance; studies have demonstrated that REE elements enhance not only the mechanical properties but also the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. REE elements improve the material’s strength properties, and due to the alloys’ good creep resistance at elevated temperatures, stable precipitates are distributed within the matrix and at grain boundaries. REE elements such as sodium (Na), potassium (K) and lithium (Li) also improve the alloy’s corrosion properties. 130 , 131 , 180  Numerous studies have demonstrated that REE elements reduce casting porosity in Mg alloys and that their formation of solid solution hardening and stable precipitates distributed within the matrix and at grain boundaries increases high-temperature strength and creep resistance. 180 , 181  Furthermore, the corrosion properties of alloys are also improved when combined with elements such as Na, K and Li.

A study conducted by Büyükgenç et al. investigates the corrosion performance and microstructural evolution of a new EZ43 Mg alloy enriched with Ce and Nd. The specimens were prepared by extrusion and subjected to corrosion testing in Hank’s solution to simulate physiological conditions. Surface characterization using scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction (XRD) was carried out, alongside electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, potentiodynamic polarisation and hydrogen evolution tests. The results demonstrated that the addition of Ce and Nd improved corrosion resistance and supported the formation of a more stable protective layer. Among the samples, EZ43B exhibited the lowest corrosion current density (Icorr) and hydrogen evolution rate, indicating superior corrosion performance. These findings indicate that REE-alloyed EZ43 Mg alloys offer significant potential for biomedical applications where lightweight and corrosion-resistant materials are required. 109

sections.heading: Biocompatibility Behaviour
paragraphs: Whilst magnesium (Mg) alloys are primarily valued for their mechanical performance and corrosion behaviour in biodegradable implant applications, their biocompatibility is also considered a critical parameter for the clinical success of the material. Biocompatible materials are those produced to assist the body’s functions and remain in contact with the body for a specific period of time. Biomaterials can typically be divided into two groups: biodegradable and non-biodegradable materials. Today, due to their good mechanical and biocompatibility properties, titanium, stainless steel and cobalt-chromium alloys are widely used as non-biodegradable materials in cardiovascular stents and orthopaedic implants for fracture surgery. Normally, it is desired that the implant used in these procedures biodegrades within the body after the healing period of the vascular or bone tissue. 33

Mg and Mg alloys are attracting significant interest as biodegradable implant materials in biological environments; this is due to their good interaction with bone, suitable mechanical properties, and the potential to convert into ions that are harmless to the body. Mg-based biodegradable implants (e.g. plates, screws, tissue scaffolds) support bone healing and subsequently dissolve, eliminating the need for a second surgical procedure; for this reason, Mg-based materials are the subject of intensive research in the fields of orthopaedics and traumatology. 182 , 183

Biomaterials consist of biocompatible products derived from various elements and compounds, including metallic compounds found naturally in the body. Recently, REE elements have attracted attention due to their intensive use in advanced studies, particularly in applications such as dental implants and orthopaedic applications, where Mg and REE elements play significant roles. Understanding the effect of these elements on biocompatibility processes in biomaterials is of vital importance. 184 ,  185 – 186

REE elements exhibit effects such as grain refinement, precipitation formation and protective layer stabilization in the Mg matrix; however, there is debate regarding the biological toxicity of some REE elements. 182 , 187  As Mg’s rapid dissolution in physiological fluids can lead to problems such as excessive hydrogen gas production and local pH elevation, the biological effects of alloying elements and corrosion products must be carefully evaluated. 117

Magnesium alloys, known for their lightness and biocompatibility, hold immense potential for biomedical applications; the addition of elements such as Zn, Nd, Ce, Gd, Zr and Ca to Mg can significantly enhance the mechanical and biological properties of these alloys. 188 , 189  In biomedical applications, the solubility of magnesium alloys in body fluids is one of the key factors determining biocompatibility. Given that physiological fluids typically have pH levels ranging from 1 to 9, it is crucial that biomaterials designed for use in the human body exhibit strong mechanical and corrosion-resistant properties. The inclusion of REE elements in these alloys has improved their suitability for biomedical applications by enhancing their biocompatibility and corrosion resistance. 190 , 191 , 193  REE additions can improve biocompatibility by regulating ion release through controlled corrosion. 47  REE additions can alter the alloy’s overall corrosion behaviour and, consequently, ion release. Low and controlled dissolution is preferred for biological acceptability, whereas rapid dissolution can lead to excessive ion release and local toxicity. REE elements can contribute to the formation of REE-oxide/hydroxide layers on the surface, providing protective layers that are more stable or have a different structure compared to the Mg(OH) 2  layer; this alters both the corrosion rate and the ion release profiles. 182  Magnesium alloys containing REE are emerging as promising materials for biomedical applications due to their lack of cytotoxicity and their ability to enhance osteoblast cell viability. 23  Mg-REE alloys are widely used in biomedical applications as biomaterials with significant potential for use, particularly in the orthopaedic and cardiovascular fields, as they are biodegradable materials that aid tissue healing and leave no residue in the body following implantation. 149

In a study conducted by Büyükgenç and colleagues, genotoxicity and cytotoxicity tests were carried out on the EZ43A and EZ43B alloys as part of biocompatibility testing. The tests examined whether the alloys disrupted the genetic structure and whether they killed bacteria. The results of the genotoxicity tests showed that genomic integrity was preserved in both alloys and that reproduction and fertilization processes continued. In the cytotoxicity tests, it was observed that the REE caused an increase of more than 142% in the bacterial count for the EZ43A alloy and an increase of 116% for the EZ43B alloy (Figure  3 ). As an increase in bacterial count exceeding 70% is considered standard for biocompatible materials, both alloys were found to be biocompatible. 109  Whilst it has been reported that Nd and Ce additions particularly facilitate good integration with bone tissue and reduce the risk of cytotoxicity, Mg is naturally present in the human body and plays a vital role in its metabolism, which makes the implants highly biocompatible. 183  It has also been reported that Nd and Ce additions form more stable surface oxide layers in a biological environment and support cell proliferation. 139  Whilst a cytotoxicity test is used to determine the effect of a test substance on cell viability, growth and division, 185 , 192 , 193  a genotoxicity test assesses the potential for DNA damage caused by a test substance. 194 , 195  These analyses detect changes in genetic material, mutations or DNA damage. 184 , 185 , 192 , 196 , 197 Figure 3 Genotoxicity test results (A) EZ43A (B) EZ43B (C) negative control (D) positive control. 109

The addition of Nd and Ce to Mg-based alloys significantly affects their biological properties, as evidenced by increased cell viability in Nd-enriched samples and the absence of genotoxic effects in all samples. 198 , 199  Statistical analysis has confirmed notable differences in the biological properties of Nd- and Ce-enriched alloys and highlighted the effect of the Nd-Ce transition on the properties of Mg-Zn matrix alloys. 10  These findings highlight the potential of Nd- and Ce-doped Mg-based alloys for biomedical applications, as they exhibit high cell viability and a non-genotoxic profile—characteristics of great importance for their use in various biomedical fields. 198 , 199

Mg alloys containing REE have been tested in numerous studies using osteoblast/osteoclast cell lines or fibroblasts; it has been reported that alloys containing low to moderate levels of REE do not inhibit cell adhesion, proliferation or differentiation, and in some cases, biocompatibility is improved. 183 , 200  In short- to medium-term animal models, some REE-Mg alloys have been reported to exhibit controlled degradation and a good tissue response; however, long-term systemic distribution and organic toxicity data remain limited. 114 , 182

Studies have shown that magnesium alloys degrade gradually within bone. The number of alloying elements and low-toxicity rare earth elements that are tolerable in the human body, biodegradable and delay the corrosion rate of magnesium alloys is limited, and research into the use of these elements in different alloy combinations is ongoing. 201 , 202

In studies conducted, scandium (Sc) stands out in the literature as one of the most biologically safe elements among REE’s. 203  The addition of holmium (Ho) to magnesium alloys, meanwhile, contributes to bone healing by promoting osteoblast proliferation. 157  However, as the accumulation of REE elements at high concentrations may lead to tissue toxicity, their use must be carefully optimized. It has been reported that magnesium alloys containing yttrium (Y) assist in the formation of a protective surface film and reduce the in vitro corrosion rate; some studies have observed good bone-implant integration in alloys containing Y. However, long-term toxicity assessments of Y ions are limited. It has been reported that Nd modification in Mg-Zn-Zr systems provides both mechanical strengthening and more balanced degradation; in vitro cell viability studies have shown positive results for some Nd-containing alloys. 114

Gd and Gd-based compounds, as well as other REE agents, are used as contrast agents in medical imaging procedures, particularly in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). 185  Gd-based contrast agents have been associated with rare cases of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis and other adverse effects. 204  However, this is rare and primarily affects individuals with pre-existing kidney problems. 205 , 206 , 210  In some studies, Gd addition has improved the mechanical, thermal and corrosion behaviour of the alloy, whilst in vitro cell studies have also shown positive results; however, caution is required regarding the systemic effects of high doses of Gd ions. 182 , 187  These findings indicate that the addition of REE to Mg alloys must be carefully optimized in terms of biocompatibility.

It has been reported that biodegradable Mg-REE stents have yielded promising results in clinical applications. 206  Preclinical animal studies indicate that Mg alloys containing REE exhibit favourable biocompatibility; however, a lack of long-term clinical data persists. 207  This situation highlights the need for more comprehensive and long-term clinical studies for the large-scale use of Mg-REE alloys in the biomedical field. Furthermore, Mg-REE alloys are also widely used in biomedical applications as a biodegradable implant material that aids tissue healing and ensures no implant residue remains. 149  Mg-REE phase diagrams demonstrate that each REE element exhibits distinct behaviour. 208  When REE elements are incorporated into alloy systems at low concentrations, they can exert positive effects on microstructure and enhance the performance of biomaterials. 203 , 207

However, these beneficial effects are dose-dependent; at high concentrations, REE accumulation may pose potential toxicity risks and lead to adverse biological outcomes. To mitigate these disadvantages, it is of great importance to carefully optimize the alloy composition and comprehensively evaluate long-term biological effects. 184 , 193 , 204 , 206 , 209 , 210

sections.heading: Applications of Mg–REE Alloys in Biomedical Engineering
paragraphs: The use of magnesium (Mg) alloys in the biomedical field has a long history. Mg was first used in 1878 for the ligation of bleeding vessels, and since then it has been extensively studied in many medical fields, including cardiovascular, musculoskeletal and general surgical applications. 211

Interest in biodegradable systems among metallic implant materials used in biomedical engineering has increased significantly in recent years, owing to the balanced combination of mechanical properties, biodegradability and biocompatibility. In this context, biodegradable Mg alloys are regarded as a new and innovative generation of biomedical metals. 212 , 213  In particular, alloys containing magnesium (Mg) and rare earth elements (REEs) are among the leading alternatives in orthopaedic and cardiovascular applications. The superior properties of Mg–REE alloys, such as biodegradability, mechanical compatibility and biocompatibility, make these materials strong candidates compared to traditional permanent implants. 45 , 139  In this context, one of the most notable application areas is orthopaedic implants, such as screws, plates and pins used in bone fixation.

Mg is an essential nutrient for the human body; it supports bone growth, enhances cell adhesion to biomaterials, and contributes to the processes of osteoblast differentiation and biomineralization. 72  Furthermore, due to their high chemical reactivity, Mg alloys can readily corrode in a physiological environment, decomposing to form magnesium hydroxide [Mg(OH) 2 ] and hydrogen gas (H 2 ). 73 , 74

From a biological perspective, it is known that rare earth elements exhibit a high affinity for bone tissue; they promote tissue regeneration by regulating bone formation and resorption processes through their direct and indirect effects on bone cells and mineral components. Furthermore, it has been reported in the literature that Mg–REE alloys exhibit antitumour and antibacterial properties. 172 , 47  The ability of these alloys to degrade in a controlled and gradual manner within a physiological environment offers the potential to eliminate the need for secondary surgical intervention, thereby reducing patient risk and healthcare costs. In cardiovascular applications, intensive research is being conducted on the use of Mg–REE alloys in biodegradable stents. The controlled degradation behaviour and improved corrosion resistance of these alloys contribute to reducing long-term complications associated with permanent metal stents, whilst providing temporary mechanical support to the vascular structure.

However, despite these promising properties, significant challenges remain, such as the precise control of the degradation rate, a full understanding of long-term biological interactions, and the optimization of the alloy composition. Consequently, more comprehensive and systematic research is required to ensure that Mg–REE-based biomaterials can be safely and effectively integrated into clinical practice.

sections.heading: Orthopaedic Applications
paragraphs: Magnesium (Mg) alloys have become a major focus in orthopaedic implant research due to their elastic moduli being similar to those of natural bone tissue, their biodegradability, and their properties that support bone repair. However, many of the biomedical Mg alloys developed to date fail to fully meet the requirements of orthopaedic applications due to their rapid degradation following implantation. 123  In contrast, biologically resorbable Mg-based alloys possessing properties such as low density, low elastic modulus and high biocompatibility are considered highly promising candidates, particularly for temporary orthopaedic implants. 96

Mg–rare earth element (Mg–REE) alloys are widely researched and used as bone implants in orthopaedic applications due to their improved mechanical properties, controlled degradation behaviour and biocompatibility. 80  These alloys offer significant advantages in temporary implants such as bone plates, screws, intramedullary nails and tissue engineering scaffolds. The fact that Mg’s elastic modulus is close to that of natural bone tissue reduces the ‘stress shielding’ effect, thereby positively influencing bone healing. Furthermore, REE additions enhance the alloy’s mechanical strength and corrosion resistance. 80 , 123  It has been reported that Mg systems alloyed with rare earth elements, particularly Gd, Nd and Y, provide adequate mechanical support during the bone healing process and exhibit controlled degradation behaviour. These alloys degrade in a manner compatible with bone tissue, thereby eliminating the need for a second surgical intervention. Furthermore, it has been reported that Mg ions enhance osteoblast activity and promote bone formation. 139

Both in vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that these alloys support bone growth and healing. In particular, in vivo studies conducted on animal models have confirmed the biocompatibility and tissue interaction of Mg–REE alloys, yielding promising results. Cytotoxicity analyses highlight the critical importance of maintaining biocompatibility in these alloys, whilst in vivo studies provide comprehensive information regarding their performance in living systems. 40

Metals play a fundamental role in clinical medicine. Traditional implant materials, such as stainless steel, cobalt-chromium alloys and titanium alloys, are widely used in orthopaedics due to their high mechanical strength, corrosion resistance and machinability. However, as these materials are biologically inert, they often require removal via secondary surgical intervention. 214  This situation imposes both an economic and psychological burden, and may also lead to complications such as tissue damage during implant removal. 215 , 216  Furthermore, the ‘stress shielding’ effect arising from their high elastic modulus can negatively impact bone healing, leading to problems such as delayed union or non-union. 217  Consequently, orthopaedic implants are expected not only to provide mechanical support but also to exhibit biologically active properties.

Mg alloys are among the new generation of biomaterials capable of meeting these requirements. Orthopaedic implants are generally divided into two groups: permanent and temporary; magnesium alloys offer significant advantages, particularly for temporary implants. These alloys are used as an effective biomaterial in the repair or replacement of damaged bone tissue. 218 , 219

However, the risk of bacterial infection in implants manufactured from biomedical magnesium alloys is a significant concern. Bacteria adhering to the implant surface can cause infection and inflammation, thereby adversely affecting the treatment process and, in some cases, necessitating revision surgery. Consequently, the development of implants with antibacterial properties has become an important area of research. To this end, the alloy composition is modified with silver, copper, zinc and rare earth elements. 220  Whilst silver ions exhibit a strong antibacterial effect, they are prone to oxidation; copper ions cause discolouration and demonstrate limited biocompatibility; zinc, meanwhile, has similar limitations. In contrast, REE’s stand out due to their high efficacy, long-term stability and broad-spectrum antibacterial properties. 139

One of the most significant limitations of Mg–REE alloys in orthopaedic applications is their rapid corrosion behaviour. However, the fine-grained structure obtained through the addition of REE and the protective passive film formed on the surface make a significant contribution to controlling the corrosion rate. 40  From a clinical perspective, the Magnezix 3.2 mm compression screw, which received the CE mark in 2013, is notable as the first Mg-based biodegradable implant to be launched on the market, and this has been followed by implants of different designs with similar compositions. 221

The first clinical studies were conducted using compression screws for the treatment of hallux valgus, and the results were reported to be equivalent to or better than those achieved with titanium alloy screws. Furthermore, successful applications have been reported in various anatomical regions, such as the mandibular condylar head, 222  radius, 223  carpus 224  and medial malleolus. 225  In these studies, it was noted that patients demonstrated complete fracture union and full functional recovery without the development of complications. Figure  4  shows the MAGNEZIX® compression screw used in a study on the fixation of medial malleolus fractures in eleven patients, viewed from different angles. 225 Figure 4 View of the MAGNEZIX® 3.2 mm compression screw from different angles. 225

In addition, the in vivo performance of JDBM screws was investigated in a goat femoral condyle fracture model for up to 18 months, and it was determined that these implants had no adverse effect on liver and kidney function. Histological analyses have shown that brushite-coated and uncoated JDBM screws promote greater new bone formation compared to the widely used polylactide (PLA). 45

One of the significant advantages of Mg-REE alloys is that their corrosion products are non-toxic and can be eliminated from the body via metabolic pathways. 233  Furthermore, these alloys degrade into harmless products once bone healing is complete and can be excreted via the circulatory system, thereby eliminating the need for a second surgical intervention. It has also been clearly demonstrated in the literature that Mg supports bone remodelling and healing. 68 , 226

In conclusion, Mg and, in particular, Mg–REE alloys stand out as highly valuable biomaterials with significant potential for orthopaedic applications, offering a unique combination of properties such as mechanical compatibility, biodegradability, biocompatibility and biological activity (Fig.  5 ). Figure 5 LAM implants with personalized structures to repair human tissues. 139

sections.heading: Cardiovascular Applications
paragraphs: Mg–REE alloys hold significant potential for applications in the cardiovascular system, particularly in biodegradable stents. Unlike traditional metal stents, Mg-based stents dissolve over time in the physiological environment, leaving no permanent foreign body within the vessel; this helps to reduce the risk of long-term complications. 40

Mg alloys containing REE can provide both the mechanical strength required for cardiovascular applications and a controlled dissolution rate. In particular, it has been reported that alloys containing neodymium (Nd) and yttrium (Y) dissolve in a manner compatible with the vessel wall, providing sufficient mechanical support for an adequate duration. Furthermore, it has been reported that these alloys promote endothelial cell proliferation and reduce the inflammatory response. 227

According to the study by Li and colleagues, Mg-REE alloys do not cause denaturation of plasma proteins or significant changes in essential blood components when in contact with blood, indicating that these materials exhibit good haemocompatibility. These findings demonstrate that Mg-REE alloys meet the requirements for in vivo use in terms of cell and blood compatibility and possess a generally safe biomaterial profile. 139

Today, the biomedical applications of magnesium alloys are primarily focussed on cardiovascular stents and orthopaedic implants. As a vascular stent, magnesium offers significant advantages such as improving blood flow, inhibiting platelet activation, preventing vasoconstriction and supporting vascular function. 228  Furthermore, magnesium-based stents provide mechanical support during the vascular remodelling process by dilating narrowed arteries, and subsequently degrade in a controlled manner, allowing natural vascular tissue to take their place. 229

A significant example of the clinical applications of magnesium alloys containing rare earth elements is the sirolimus-eluting, balloon-expandable Magmaris (formerly known as DREAMS 2G) stent, which received CE marking in 2016. 230  With clinical studies dating back to 2005, this system is one of the earliest clinical applications of Mg alloys containing biodegradable REE and has a substantial body of clinical data. One of the first products used in this system was a laser-cut bare-metal stent manufactured from the WE43 alloy. Following successful preclinical results in porcine models, 214  these stents were tested on 20 patients with critical limb ischaemia (CLI), yielding highly successful outcomes such as a 100% limb salvage rate. 231  Subsequently, in the PROGRESS AMS-1 clinical trial, similar positive results were observed in 63 patients, and it was reported that the performance was comparable to that of current biodegradable polymer stents. 232

Experimental studies on the degradation behaviour and biological effects of magnesium alloys also support the potential of these materials. In a study conducted by Kraus et al., the in vivo degradation behaviour of ZX50, which does not contain REE, and WZ21, which contains Y, was compared. Whilst the WZ21 alloy exhibited more controlled and linear degradation, it was observed that the ZX50 alloy underwent rapid corrosion causing a high level of gas formation. Furthermore, it has been determined that the addition of Y not only enhances corrosion resistance but also promotes new bone formation around the implant and preserves tissue integrity. 233

Cardiovascular stents, which are widely used in clinical practice today, are generally manufactured from permanent biomaterials such as stainless steel or cobalt-chromium alloys. However, the prolonged presence of these materials in the body can lead to late-stage complications. For this reason, Mg–REE alloys containing rare earth elements such as yttrium and neodymium are emerging as an alternative solution.

In the cardiovascular applications of Mg–REE alloys, stents manufactured from these alloys are gaining prominence. These stents provide the necessary mechanical support throughout the vascular healing process and then degrade in a controlled manner, eventually being expelled from the body. This eliminates the need for a permanent implant, thereby reducing the risk of long-term complications and the need for further surgical intervention. Furthermore, the degradation kinetics can be optimized to align with the vascular healing process. Furthermore, the inclusion of rare earth elements in the alloy improves the material’s interaction with blood and surrounding tissues, thereby enhancing biocompatibility. This contributes to a reduction in immune responses and supports endothelial healing. 234 , 235  For example, a Mg–REE alloy stent implanted in a patient with arterial stenosis provides temporary support during the vascular healing process before completely dissolving and disappearing, thereby allowing the natural vascular structure to regenerate. 236
Consequently, Mg–REE alloys rank among the most promising biomaterials for cardiovascular applications due to their controlled degradability, suitable mechanical properties and high biocompatibility.

sections.heading: Tissue Engineering and Skeletal Systems
paragraphs: Mg–REE alloys offer significant potential in tissue engineering applications, particularly as porous scaffold structures. Such structures support tissue repair processes by providing a suitable microenvironment for cell adhesion, proliferation and tissue regeneration. Porous Mg–REE structures provide sufficient mechanical support whilst, at the same time, creating the necessary space for new tissue formation through their controlled degradation behaviour. 139

The osteogenic properties of Mg–REE alloys are closely related to the biological effects of ions released from Mg and rare earth elements. Studies by Zheng, Qin and other researchers have demonstrated that these ions stimulate sensory nerve endings in the periosteal region, triggering the release of neurotransmitters and thereby promoting the osteogenic differentiation of stem cells present in the periosteum. 237  This mechanism explains why Mg–REE alloys are effective biomaterials for bone regeneration.

Thanks to the regulatory effect of rare earth elements on the microstructure of the alloy, a more homogeneous pore distribution and enhanced mechanical stability can be achieved in Mg–REE systems. This improves both the mechanical strength and the biological performance of the scaffold. Furthermore, it is known that Mg ions released during the biodegradation process support cellular activities and accelerate tissue regeneration. 45

In the treatment of tumour-induced bone defects, although surgical resection is a widely used method, the presence of residual tumour cells carries a risk of recurrence. Therefore, it is of great importance that implant materials not only provide structural support but also possess antitumour properties. In this context, Mg–REE alloys offer a promising approach. The high charge-to-ion-radius ratio of rare earth elements enables strong binding to divalent metal ions found in tumour cell mitochondria, and this interaction gives rise to an antitumour effect. 238

Consequently, Mg–REE alloys stand out as versatile and innovative biomaterials in tissue engineering and skeletal system applications due to their controlled degradability, osteogenic effects, biocompatibility and potential antitumour properties.

sections.heading: New Generation Manufacturing Technologies and Applications
paragraphs: In recent years, advanced manufacturing technologies such as additive manufacturing have significantly expanded the scope of applications for Mg–REE alloys in biomedical fields. These methods enable the design of patient-specific implants and allow for highly precise control over the material’s microstructure. In particular, it has been demonstrated that mechanical properties and corrosion behaviour can be optimized in alloys such as Mg–Nd through rapid solidification processes.

In this context, laser additive manufacturing (LAM) has emerged as one of the advanced manufacturing techniques attracting significant attention in recent years. LAM offers an advanced manufacturing approach that combines high performance with high-precision shaping by enabling precise control of personalized external geometries and internal structures. 139 , 239  In this technique, three-dimensional computer-aided design (CAD) models are sliced into layers at the micrometre scale, and metal powders are melted layer by layer using a laser beam to produce clearly defined parts with complex geometries.

Compared to other production methods, LAM offers a number of advantages: these include simplification of the production process and material savings, reduction of costs and production time by eliminating the need for moulds, the ability to achieve fine microstructures thanks to rapid melting and solidification, the ability to produce complex and porous structures, and the provision of high machining accuracy. For example, the production of scaffold structures made from WE43 alloy using the LAM method has successfully resulted in highly porous and fully interconnected porous architectures. 240  The fact that the geometric accuracy of the resulting structures is very close to the designed model clearly demonstrates the superior shaping capability of this method. Such advanced manufacturing techniques offer new possibilities in implant design, contributing to the development of patient-specific solutions and the improvement of treatment outcomes.

With the growing interest in biodegradable metal implants, these alloys are emerging as an alternative to inert metal implants and are regarded as a promising solution in modern medical applications. Furthermore, by combining advanced characterization techniques with thermal and phase-field modelling approaches, complex structural features such as banded microstructure formation in Mg–REE alloys during the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) process have been examined in detail. 96

Consequently, additive manufacturing technologies are enhancing the performance of Mg–REE alloys in biomedical applications and opening up new horizons, particularly in terms of the production of customized implants, controlled microstructure design and functional optimization.

sections.heading: Clinical Potential and Limitations
paragraphs: It has been reported that Mg alloys developed with low and optimized REE additions exhibit balanced performance in terms of mechanical strength, corrosion resistance and biocompatibility. This suggests that these alloys have the potential for wider clinical use in the future. 40

Furthermore, the biological effects of rare earth elements are not limited solely to mechanical and structural properties. The literature reports that REE exhibit antimicrobial effects against bacteria and yeast/fungal species. 241  This property offers a significant advantage, particularly in topical applications for burn treatments 173  and the development of antibacterial implant materials. 242

However, the clinical use of magnesium-based alloys remains limited, and the number of medical devices based on Mg alloys containing rare earth elements is also relatively small. 45  Despite the clinical potential of Mg–REE alloys, there are some significant limitations. In particular, the use of rare earth elements at high concentrations may increase the risk of local toxicity. Furthermore, the lack of long-term in vivo studies stands out as one of the key factors slowing the transition of these materials to widespread clinical applications. 96

In conclusion, whilst Mg–REE alloys possess high clinical potential, issues such as toxicity control, the enhancement of long-term biocompatibility data, and alloy optimization require more detailed consideration. Advanced research in these areas will pave the way for the more widespread and safe use of Mg–REE-based biomaterials in clinical applications.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: In general, Mg–REE alloys are considered highly promising candidates for biodegradable implant applications, and the findings clearly demonstrate that alloying magnesium (Mg) with rare earth elements (REE) is an effective strategy for enhancing the overall performance of biodegradable Mg alloys. Future research should focus on the systematic optimization of alloy design and comprehensive biological evaluations to ensure that these materials can be used safely and effectively in clinical applications.
The results obtained from this study are listed as follows:

The addition of REEs to Mg alloys is emerging as a promising approach that offers new opportunities in biomaterial research from both microstructural and biological perspectives. REEs can have significant effects on Mg alloys in terms of mechanical properties, microstructure, and corrosion; when optimized correctly, these changes provide a marked improvement in biocompatibility. Magnesium alloys are susceptible to various corrosion mechanisms, including galvanic corrosion, localized corrosion, friction corrosion, stress corrosion cracking and corrosion fatigue. REE types such as Nd and Ce increase mechanical strength through grain refinement and precipitation formation, while also increasing corrosion resistance and supporting biocompatibility. It has been reported that the addition of strontium (Sr) to form an alloy with magnesium enhances the mechanical, tribological and corrosion properties of the magnesium alloy; furthermore, it has been reported that it improves the grain structure of the alloy, reduces shrinkage and increases porosity. REE addition offers significant potential for industrial and biomedical applications of Mg alloys. However, the potential systemic effects of REE elements, their ion release profiles, and long-term in vivo behaviour remain poorly understood. Recent research and studies have shown that adding elements such as Nd, Ce, Gd, and Sc to Mg alloys at low concentrations provides multiple benefits, including improving the mechanical properties of the alloys, reducing the corrosion rate, and enhancing cell viability to impart a biocompatible structure. Although Mg-based materials possess advantages such as low density and an elastic modulus close to that of bone tissue, they generally fail to demonstrate sufficient performance in implant applications due to low ductility and limited strength.
